question: A 10-week-old infant develops a 3 cm indurated, painful abscess at the BCG injection site 3 weeks after vaccination. The vaccine was given at the correct intradermal site in the left deltoid region. Which AEFI category does this most likely represent?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A vaccine product-related reaction is caused by inherent properties of the vaccine (e.g., fever from DTP). A localised abscess 3 weeks post-BCG with a history of correct technique is more consistent with a programme error.

A vaccine quality defect (e.g., contamination at manufacture) would typically affect multiple recipients from the same batch. A single case with correct administration technique points to a different cause.

Correct. An indurated abscess developing at the BCG site, despite apparently correct deltoid placement, suggests a subcutaneous rather than true intradermal injection — a programme (technique) error. BCG given subcutaneously causes a cold abscess. This is classified as an immunization error-related AEFI and is reportable.

A coincidental event has no causal link to vaccination (e.g., a febrile illness from an unrelated infection occurring post-vaccination). A localised abscess at the injection site has a direct anatomical link to the vaccination procedure.

overallFeedback.feedback: AEFI classification: product-related (inherent vaccine properties), quality defect (manufacturing), programme error (administration technique/cold chain), coincidental (unrelated event), unknown. Localised BCG abscess = programme error.
BCG abscess at the injection site after apparently correct technique = programme error (subcutaneous rather than intradermal injection). Report as immunization error-related AEFI.
